fixes.explanation: Steady it is. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends (Job 2:11), says, “Your words have steadied those who stumbled…” (Job 4:4). He adds that Job braced knees that were buckling. So Job was the one folks leaned on when their legs went wobbly, and that's a great thing to be known for.

Scold sounds like a finger-wagging lecture, but that's not what Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends (Job 2:11), says. He says Job's words “…steadied those who stumbled…” (Job 4:4). He also says Job strengthened feeble hands (Job 4:3). I'd take a friend like that any day of the week.

Scatter is how my sprinkles behave when I bump the jar, not what Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends (Job 2:11), says about Job. He says Job's words “…steadied those who stumbled…” (Job 4:4). He also says Job strengthened feeble hands and braced knees that were buckling. Steadying is a long way from scattering.

Kings never show up in this verse. Eliphaz pleads with Job, “Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” (Job 4:7). His question is about the innocent and the upright. Crowns and thrones aren't in it.

Yes, the breath of God. Eliphaz says, “By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.” (Job 4:9). He's talking about those who plow iniquity and sow trouble, who he says reap the same (Job 4:8). Those are his words, so we hear them as his claim.

That's the question. The voice asks, “Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?” (Job 4:17). Eliphaz says it came in disquieting visions in the night, as a whispering voice. That's what he reports hearing.

The voice goes the other way. It says, “If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay…” (Job 4:18-19). The words “…how much more…” push the point onto people, and not in a flattering direction. The voice says people dwell in houses of clay, with foundations in the dust.

That's right. Eliphaz says, “The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.” (Job 5:5). They take it even from the thorns. That's the picture he paints of the cursed fool.

Nothing rots in this verse. Eliphaz says, “The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns…” (Job 5:5). People take it, and they even reach into the thorns to do it. Rotting isn't what he describes.

The text says the opposite. Eliphaz says, “For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground.” (Job 5:6). Trouble doesn't pop up out of the dirt like a weed. Right after that he says man is born to trouble (Job 5:7).

Yes. Eliphaz says, “However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him…” (Job 5:8). That's what he says he'd do in Job's place. Then he goes on to talk about the One who does great and unsearchable things (Job 5:9).

The text says it's true. Eliphaz says, “For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.” (Job 5:18). The wounding and striking are paired with binding and healing in the same breath. If you only caught the first half, I get it, but the whole verse has both.

Laugh is it. Eliphaz tells Job, “You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.” (Job 5:22). That's quite a promise to make to a man who has lost so much (Job 1:13–19). Whatever you think of Eliphaz's words, the laughing is what he says.

Alone and forgotten isn't what Eliphaz says. He says, “You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.” (Job 5:26). Full vigor is how he says Job will come. The grain is gathered right in season.
